papers.title: Interictal Electroencephalographic Characteristics of the Human Centromedian Thalamic Nucleus Recorded in Focal Epilepsy.
papers.abstract: The centromedian (CM) thalamic nucleus is critical in sleep-wake regulation and epileptic networks; yet its electroencephalography (EEG) characteristics remain incompletely understood. CM EEG across vigilance states and interictal epileptic discharges (IEDs) in focal epilepsy were investigated. Interictal stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) recordings from the CM and neighboring ventroposterior (VP) and ventrolateral (VL) nuclei were analyzed with synchronous cortical SEEG and scalp EEG during wakefulness, non-rapid eye movement sleep, rapid eye movement sleep, and spontaneous non-epileptic arousal. Spectral power was quantified across frequency bands. Sleep-related thalamic activities and thalamic IEDs were visually identified. SEEG data from 33 patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy and 3 non-epileptic individuals were analyzed. CM exhibited continuous fast activity during wakefulness and delta/theta-dominant activity during sleep, confirmed by increased gamma-fast ripple power in wakefulness and enhanced delta/theta power in sleep (all p < 0.014). During spontaneous non-epileptic arousal, thalamic EEG changes preceded scalp EEG arousal (median 800 ms; interquartile range: 400-1500 ms). Four sleep-related thalamic EEG activities were reproducibly observed in non-epileptic individuals, supporting a potential physiological nature. Thalamic IEDs occurred in 36.4% of patients with focal epilepsy, invariably involved the CM. Thalamic IEDs were more frequent in extratemporal than temporal lobe epilepsy and were not associated with surgical outcome. CM SEEG demonstrates distinct, state-dependent electrophysiological dynamics across the sleep-wake cycle and preferential involvement in interictal epileptic activity compared with VL/VP nuclei. These findings lay the foundation for a thalamic EEG atlas and refine understanding of differential engagement of thalamic nuclei in epileptic networks.

papers.title: Chronic neuropeptide S treatment improves sleep architecture and reduces Aβ-related pathology in APP/PS1 mice.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances frequently occur in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Although neuropeptide S (NPS) promotes wakefulness through the widely expressed NPS receptor (NPSR), its role in AD-related sleep dysregulation is unclear. To investigate the effects of chronic NPS administration on AD-related sleep disturbances beyond its acute wake-promoting effects. NPSR expression was examined in the hypothalamus and hippocampus of APPswe/PS1dE9 (APP/PS1) mice, a double-transgenic mouse model of AD. Mice received intracerebroventricular NPS (1 nmol/day) for 14 days. Sleep-wake states were classified as wakefulness, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Sleep architecture and amyloid-β (Aβ)-related pathology were assessed in mice. Cell-associated Aβ levels, extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) phosphorylation, and autophagy-related proteins were examined in BV2 cells. Sleep responses to subsequent intracerebroventricular Aβ₁-₄₂ administration were examined in NPS-treated APP/PS1 mice. APP/PS1 mice had lower NPSR protein levels in the hypothalamus and hippocampus than wild-type (WT) controls. Compared with saline-treated APP/PS1 mice, NPS-treated mice showed increased NREM sleep, reduced wakefulness, and lower Aβ-related pathology. Changes in sleep amounts were most evident during the light phase. Subsequent Aβ₁-₄₂ administration increased wakefulness and reduced NREM sleep mainly during the dark phase. It also shortened NREM episodes during the light phase. In BV2 cells, NPS altered cell-associated Aβ levels and increased ERK phosphorylation. NPS treatment was also associated with higher LC3B-II and lower p62 levels. SCH772984 attenuated the NPS-associated changes in autophagy-related proteins and cell-associated Aβ. Chronic NPS administration improved sleep architecture and reduced Aβ-related pathology in APP/PS1 mice. The BV2 findings suggest possible involvement of ERK signaling and autophagy-related processes in cellular Aβ handling.

papers.title: Using wearable EEG to examine age trends in sleep macro- and micro-architecture across adolescence
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a period of distinct maturational changes in sleep physiology. Age-related trends in sleep physiology have been captured using laboratory-based polysomnography, a method limited by logistical burden and high cost. We tested the ability of the Dreem3 sleep EEG headband to replicate established age effects in sleep physiology from late childhood through early adulthood. Typically developing youth (N=100, 9-26 years) completed 3-4 consecutive nights of at-home sleep recording. We estimated age-related trends across eight macro-architecture and 15 micro-architecture variables with known age effects and conducted exploratory analyses of 24 additional variables. The Dreem3 replicated some established age trends, including increases in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) stage 2%, and decreases in N3%, time in bed, NREM delta and theta power with increasing age. Although not all expected age-related associations reached statistical significance, like total sleep time and sleep efficiency, effect estimates were largely in the expected direction. These findings highlight the promise of wearable EEG devices for characterizing developmental sleep physiology while underscoring the need for further validation across sleep measures and age groups.

papers.title: Detection of linear dependencies in EEG oscillatory sources via PARALIND and block-term decomposition: A comparative study.
papers.abstract: Narrowband oscillatory rhythms in electroencephalogram (EEG) signals are fundamental signatures of neural dynamics, crucial for brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) and monitoring neurological disorders. While traditionally detected and analyzed via Independent or Principal Component Analysis in the time-space domain, tensor decomposition in the time-space-frequency domain offers superior resolution. The CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) model is widely used for this purpose due to itssimplicity and interpretability. However, it often fails to resolve rhythms or requires excessive components when source collinearity exists (i.e., a situation where oscillatory rhythms share characteristics across temporal, spatial, or frequency modes), leading to instability and increased computational complexity.Approach: This study evaluates two alternative tensor decomposition models - Parallel Profiles with Linear Dependencies (PARALIND) and Block-Term Decomposition (BTD) - which explicitly accommodate linear dependencies among latent components. We compared these models against CP using simulated EEG data with known ground-truth structures and real-world recordings.Main results: PARALIND and BTD achieved interpretability comparable to CP while providing more stable factor estimates at moderate noise levels in simulated data, although both models struggled to identify the true latent structure under challenging conditions. Overall, when their modelling assumptions were satisfied, PARALIND and BTD successfully disentangled complex, overlapping neural sources that CP struggled to isolate. In real data, both models recovered a latent structure similar to that identified by CP, but with fewer loadings. Following the principle of parsimony, PARALIND and BTD may therefore be preferable in this setting.Significance: By overcoming the collinearity limitations inherent in CP decomposition, these findings establish a more reliable framework for neurophysiologically interpretable tensor decomposition of EEG signals. While clinical translation was not evaluated in this work, this methodological advance provides a foundation for future research aimed at enhancing BCI stability and investigating biomarkers of neurological conditions.

papers.title: In-ear electroencephalography: a systematic review of technology, applications, challenges, and future directions.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used to monitor brain activity in both clinical and research settings. However, conventional scalp EEG systems require multiple electrodes, specialised equipment, and trained personnel, which limits their practicality for long-term monitoring in everyday environments. In-ear EEG has emerged as a promising wearable alternative that enables discreet and portable neural monitoring. This systematic review examines the current state of research on in-ear EEG technologies. Twenty-four studies met the inclusion criteria and were analysed thematically. The literature highlights rapid progress in device miniaturisation and wearable design, with reported applications including sleep monitoring, seizure detection, cognitive workload assessment, fatigue monitoring, and emotion recognition. Despite these advances, challenges remain related to signal quality, spatial coverage, and motion artefacts. Further research is required to validate in-ear EEG for broader clinical and real-world applications.

papers.title: Macroscale dynamics of EEG microstates constitute the periodic and aperiodic features of the neural power spectrum
papers.abstract: The global signal characteristics of scalp-recorded electroencephalography (EEG) are composed of periodic oscillatory rhythms and aperiodic broadband fluctuations that together comprise the neural power spectrum. Spectral decomposition of these features has long served as the primary window into the macroscale characteristics of human brain activity. Here, we propose that the primary periodic rhythms and majority share of broadband spectral power within the brain's dominant frequencies are the frequency-domain representations of the dynamics of EEG microstates. Microstates are characterized by a small repertoire of topographic voltage configurations that each reflect the momentary functional state of the cortex, and it is their time-domain dynamics that mathematically constitute periodic and aperiodic spectral features. We isolated and removed the spatial projections of distinct microstate configurations from high-density EEG using orthogonal subspace projection applied to both the surface scalp recordings and their modeled cortical generators to computationally test this dependency. Spectral parameterization of the residual power spectral density revealed that removing these spatial projections strongly attenuated alpha and theta rhythms and features of the aperiodic 1/f background. Selectively removing specific microstate configurations also demonstrated that each configuration aligned with spatially specific oscillatory and aperiodic 1/f components. Furthermore, correlational analyses of microstate temporal dynamics demonstrated that the average duration and temporal persistence of microstates strongly correlate with periodic alpha power, theta power, and the aperiodic 1/f background. Our findings suggest that dominant periodic and aperiodic spectral features are more accurately understood as the frequency-domain expressions of the dynamics of EEG microstates.

papers.title: Temporal-context learning for subject-independent sleep staging with non-contact multi-frequency radar.
papers.abstract: Contactless radar may support unobtrusive sleep monitoring, but reliable five-stage evaluation requires participant-isolated testing and a clear assessment of the contribution of model components. The analysis included all 32 overnight recordings (33 964 labelled 30 s epochs) in the PhysioNet Sleep Bioradiolocation Database. Eight documented I/Q channel pairs spanning 3.6-4.0 GHz underwent complex clutter suppression, phase demodulation, fixed 0.05-0.70 Hz zero-phase filtering and resampling to 10 Hz. A 266 342-parameter composite network combined a shared one-dimensional encoder, cross-frequency contrastive initialization, quality-conditioned frequency fusion and a bidirectional gated recurrent unit over nine epochs. Eight deterministic folds each used 24 training, four validation and four held-out test participants, so every participant was tested once. Primary outcomes were participant-level five-stage macro-F1, balanced accuracy and Cohen's kappa. The full network achieved accuracy 0.434, macro-F1 0.376 (95% confidence interval 0.344-0.409), balanced accuracy 0.432 (0.405-0.457) and kappa 0.271 (0.235-0.308). Removing temporal context reduced macro-F1 by 0.072 (0.050-0.095), whereas neither contrastive initialization nor learned fusion showed an incremental held-out benefit. An independently trained early-fusion CNN-BiGRU achieved macro-F1 0.296. The participant-isolated evaluation identifies temporal context as the main contributor among the assessed components and provides a reproducible reference for future radar-based sleep-staging studies.

papers.title: A Breathable Nanomesh-Textile Electrode Interface for Integrated Multimodal Monitoring.
papers.abstract: Long-term wearable electrophysiology requires electrodes that are skin-conformal, breathable, mechanically stable, and reliably connected to electronics. Existing dry electrodes address parts of this challenge, but the interface between soft electrodes and wearable electronics remains a major source of motion artifacts, open-circuit failure, and poor long-term usability. Here, we introduce a duo-electrode interface that separates the functions of skin contact and electronic interconnection. An electrospun nanomesh serves as a tattoo electrode that conforms intimately to the skin, while a compressible conductive taffeta-foam fabric electrode embedded in a garment provides stable electrical coupling to textile-routed electronics. This architecture preserves the advantages of skin-conformal electrodes while avoiding fragile connections to electronics. We integrate the interface into a bodysuit and eyemask platform for multimodal monitoring of ECG, EMG, EOG, and body position using a centralized electronics module. The system maintains reliable signal acquisition under body motion and muscle activation, with performance comparable to or better than that of commercial hydrogel electrodes. By bridging breathable electrodes with textile-based routing, the proposed duo-electrode strategy establishes a practical method for scalable, comfortable, and long-duration wearable bioelectronic monitoring. This approach may be broadly useful for remote healthcare, rehabilitation, sleep studies, human-machine interfaces, and personalized physiological sensing.

papers.title: Time of day metabolism and endocrine regulation of immune health.
papers.abstract: The immune system is a dynamic, energy-dependent network regulated by temporal biology. Advances in circadian biology have enabled the synchronizing of critical immune parameters such as metabolism, endocrine secretions, surveillance, tissue repair, and adaptation to environmental cycles. Here, we propose a metabolomic, and endocrine, chromodynamic model of immune health, based on time-of-day rhythms. Immune resilience is defined by synchronization among three groups of oscillators i) the central circadian clocks, ii) food-entrainable metabolic oscillators, iii) peripheral cellular clocks. The model provides a framework to optimize these interconnected systems to maintain metabolic efficiency, minimize unnecessary inflammation, and enable precise immune responses through temporal gating. External factors of modern lifestyle disruptions, including irregular feeding patterns, sleep deprivation, and chronic stress, induce internal circadian desynchrony, contributing to persistent low-grade inflammation, metabolic dysfunction, immune aging, and chronic non-communicable diseases. We propose that immune health is characterized not merely by the absence of disease, but by stable circadian phase coherence, low inflammatory noise, and adaptive immune resilience. We have listed some chrono-biomarkers of metabolomic and endocrine parameters that may provide a functional assessment of immune resilience, defined by inflammatory tone, immune adaptability, metabolic integrity, and repair capacity. This framework integrates chronobiology, endocrine and immunometabolism to shift medicine from reactive disease management toward proactive assessment and restoration of biological resilience.

papers.title: Cortical depth EEG-fMRI at 7T: Experimental setup and analysis pipeline to elucidate generating mechanisms of alpha oscillations.
papers.abstract: Alpha band (8-13 Hz) electroencephalography (EEG) oscillations are central to cognition, but their generating mechanisms are poorly understood. Most laminar studies investigating origins of alpha oscillations rely on invasive animal intracranial recordings. To relate these findings to human alpha generation, non-invasive techniques need to be developed. Ultra-high-field (UHF, 7T) laminar functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) enables cortical depth resolved brain responses, and, combined with simultaneous EEG, offers new insight into human alpha generation mechanisms. This work presents a framework for studying the generating mechanisms of electrophysiological signals non-invasively in humans using simultaneous EEG laminar fMRI. Data were acquired on 10 participants during an eyes-closed/eyes-open paradigm. In 9 of 10 participants, the quality of EEG and Blood Oxygenation Level Dependent (BOLD) fMRI data were sufficient to observe a significant negative correlation between EEG alpha power and the BOLD signal in visual cortex grey matter. To improve depth specificity and mitigate pial-surface BOLD signal increases due to draining veins, we applied "deveining". The effects of each of the deveining analysis steps on the cortical depth profiles of the negative alpha-BOLD correlations were studied. The largest effect arose from excluding voxels in the tissue immediately surrounding veins. After deveining, the negative alpha-BOLD correlations were significantly weaker in the middle cortical depths than in superficial and deep depths. This depth dependence was absent when modelling the task with a boxcar regressor rather than EEG alpha power, suggesting specificity to spontaneous electrophysiological (alpha) fluctuations. In conclusion, we have established a method to non-invasively interrogate the origins of electrophysiological signals. Our alpha-BOLD depth profiles during the eyes-open/eyes-closed task (strongest correlations in superficial and deep layers) are consistent with activity in cortical depths typically associated with feedback/top-down processing, but we cannot definitively demonstrate causality from these data.

papers.title: Circadian rhythm dysregulation and brain functional connectivity alterations in stroke patients: an exploratory study of peripheral and central clock interactions.
papers.abstract: The human circadian rhythm system is governed by a transcriptional-translational feedback loop of clock genes, including Bmal1, which exhibits a near-24-hour oscillatory period. Emerging evidence highlights the critical contribution of circadian genes to stroke pathogenesis and outcomes, yet mechanistic insights into their regulatory roles remain limited. To bridge this knowledge gap, we aimed to determine whether the serum of stroke patients could affect changes in the molecular clock and whether such changes in the molecular clock were potentially linked to abnormal brain functional connectivity in stroke patients. This prospective case-control study included 17 patients with stroke and 17 age-matched healthy participants. All participants were required to complete a standardized comprehensive questionnaire. Transfected human osteosarcoma cells (U2OS) stably expressing Bmal1-dluc reporters were treated with serum from both groups to monitor changes in the daily oscillation period of Bmal1. We also compared the changes in resting-state hypothalamic intrinsic functional connectivity(FC) between the two groups. Further, we explored the correlation between the differences in FC between the two groups and the daily oscillation period of Bmal1. Compared to the healthy control group, stroke patients exhibited a significantly prolonged peripheral Bmal1 circadian oscillation period (24.32 ± 0.41 h vs. 23.81 ± 0.48 h, t = 3.352, p = 0.002). In FC analysis, the stroke group showed enhanced connectivity from the hypothalamus to the right occipital lobe and the right insular region. Notably, the degree of this connectivity enhancement demonstrated a significant positive correlation with the length of Bmal1 oscillation period (r = 0.369, p = 0.032; r = 0.393, p = 0.022). Our findings suggest that serum from stroke patients lengthens the circadian period in U2OS cells and may be associated with alterations in brain functional connectivity. However, the small sample size limits statistical power, and these exploratory results require replication in larger independent cohorts. ChiCTR2000031671(April 4, 2020).

papers.title: Linking ferroptosis to chronic sleep deprivation: emerging insights into mechanisms and interventions.
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for maintaining systemic homeostasis, facilitating tissue repair, and consolidating neural circuitry. In modern society, however, accelerated lifestyles and rising work pressures have made sleep deprivation (SD) a pressing public health concern. Recent studies increasingly link chronic sleep deprivation (CSD) to various neurological disorders. The precise mechanisms, however, are not fully understood. Notably, ferroptosis as a regulated form of cell death has emerged as a potential link between CSD and neurodegeneration. This narrative review critically synthesizes evidence linking CSD with ferroptosis, with particular emphasis on iron handling, lipid peroxidation, the system Xc - -GSH-GPX4 defense axis, mitochondrial/redox stress, and neuroinflammatory signaling. Furthermore, previous studies suggest that interventions such as ketogenic diets, ω-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, vitamin B6 and phytochemicals supplementation can modulate ferroptosis in CSD mouse model. Therefore, they may serve as potential nutritional and pharmacological therapeutic targets. However, current evidence remains predominantly preclinical, and many studies rely on ferroptosis-associated biomarkers rather than definitive causal tests. A deeper understanding of the mechanistic interplay between ferroptosis and CSD will not only advance our comprehension of CSD-induced neural impairment, but also provide a theoretical basis for the development of novel therapeutic strategies for sleep-related disorders.

papers.title: Scalp EEG seizure warning in children under a pre-specified, locked evaluation: confound audit, structured chance levels and a negative result
papers.abstract: Reported performance of scalp electroencephalographic (EEG) seizure prediction is often inflated by lenient evaluation and by the vigilance-state, clock-time and admission-trend structure of monitoring data. We asked how much short-horizon warning survives a pre-specified, locked evaluation. Continuous video-EEG from 21 monitored children (1315 h) formed the development cohort. A statistical-process-control warning method, evaluated under a written protocol, detected 44% of evaluable seizures at 0.48 false alarms per hour, no better than a random predictor (51%, p = 0.86); its statistic moved three times more with vigilance state than with seizure approach. We re-designed it as a state-conditioned, directional scheme on seven global EEG features, froze it with a hash-recorded configuration and time-stamped pre-specification, and estimated its performance by nested leave-one-patient-out cross-validation: 15 of 45 seizures (33%) at 0.47 false alarms per hour, above analytic (21%, p = 0.034) and permutation chance, but a predictor using only clock time, vigilance state and days since admission reproduced most of this, and the signal was confined to the last 30 min. Applied once to two validation cohorts (a second batch from the same unit and the public CHB-MIT database; 101 evaluable seizures), the frozen scheme detected 19 seizures (19%) at 0.60 false alarms per hour against 26% chance (p = 0.96); no secondary endpoint was met, and with the child as the unit of analysis no cohort was above chance. Scalp-EEG warning should be evaluated under pre-specified rules against structured chance levels; the frozen scheme and framework are offered as a reference.

papers.title: Electroencephalography Neurophysiology Alterations in Association with Aβ and Tau Pathology Across the Symptomatic Stages of Alzheimer's Disease Continuum: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau deposition drive Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, how these proteinopathies are linked to macroscopic neural activity alterations measured by electroencephalography (EEG) in symptomatic AD remains inadequately characterized. This study aims to investigate the associations between Aβ, tau, EEG neurophysiology, and cognition. We conducted a cross-sectional study of 73 MCI and AD participants, who underwent resting-state EEG, Aβ-PET, and tau-PET. EEG source analysis was performed to extract regional spectral power. Linear mixed-effects models were used to examine the associations of regional Aβ (quantified by SUVR), tau (binary classification), with EEG features, controlling for age, sex and education. Ordinary least squares (OLS) regression was applied to investigate the relationships of EEG spectral power and global Aβ burden with cognitive performance. Elevated Aβ burden was associated with distinct regional spectral alterations. Specifically, higher Aβ SUVR was significantly correlated with increased theta power and decreased beta power in a subset of cortical regions. Tau positivity did not modulate the amyloid-theta association in any region, but attenuated the amyloid-beta association in a small set of parietal regions. We identified a localized pattern of Aβ-related neurophysiological dysfunction across the symptomatic stages of AD continuum, characterized by theta increases and beta decreases, supporting a robust association between Aβ burden and cortical neural slowing. The findings highlight the value of source-localized EEG power as a sensitive indicator of Aβ-associated network dysfunction in AD and underscore the potential of source-localized EEG as a complementary, non-invasive biomarker for assessing pathological burden and informing diagnostic strategies in AD.

papers.title: Acute intermittent carotid body stimulations induce long-term facilitation of respiratory-cardiovascular coupling in rats.
papers.abstract: Hypertension, the leading modifiable risk factor for global mortality, is driven in >50% of cases by neurogenic mechanisms linked to heightened sympathetic nerve activity (SNA). A hallmark of neurogenic hypertension is the exacerbation of respiratory-modulated SNA (RespSNA) and resulting blood pressure Traube-Hering (TH) waves, which emerges during the prehypertensive period and contributes to disease development. Carotid bodies (CBs), the peripheral chemoreceptors involved in the hypoxic response, are hyperactive in hypertensive patients and animal models. Their chronic intermittent stimulation, as seen in obstructive sleep apnoea, promotes hypertension characterised by exacerbated RespSNA and TH waves. Yet, their causal role in initiating these changes remains unclear. Here, we investigated whether acute intermittent CB stimulations could directly enhance RespSNA, TH waves and blood pressure from a physiological baseline, using the in situ working heart-brainstem preparation in rats. Four brief CB stimulations with sodium cyanide, mimicking acute intermittent hypoxia, were sufficient to induce a prolonged (>20 min) increase in both inspiratory and late expiratory RespSNA bursts, TH waves and perfusion pressure, with these effects being prevented by carotid sinus denervation. These changes were accompanied by a reconfiguration of central respiratory and cardiovascular control, including elevated respiratory heart rate variability and enhanced respiratory drive targeting upper airway and abdominal muscles. Our findings demonstrate that acute intermittent CB activation triggers sustained RespSNA and elevation of TH waves, supporting its potential role in development of hypertension. Our data also suggest that CBs play a key role in initiating this respiratory-cardiovascular plasticity and that central mechanisms might contribute to its long-term maintenance. KEY POINTS: Carotid body (CB) overactivity is implicated in sympathetic excitation and development of hypertension, but its direct role in initiating respiratory-cardiovascular dysfunction remains unresolved. We tested whether brief, repeated CB stimulations could trigger lasting changes in breathing and blood pressure control from a physiological baseline. In rats, only four stimulations induced a persistent increase in respiratory-modulated sympathetic activity, elevating blood pressure fluctuations (Traube-Hering waves) and mean blood pressure. These effects, prevented by carotid sinus denervation, were linked to enhanced respiratory-cardiovascular coupling and altered upper airway and abdominal motor control. Our findings reveal that short-term CB activation can induce long-term facilitation of respiratory-cardiovascular coupling, relevant to both physiological adaptations and hypertension pathogenesis.

papers.title: Multimodal EEG-fNIRS complexity analysis can reveal the neurovascular coupling change with aging.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate age-related changes in neurovascular coupling (NVC) function of the brain using a multimodal electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) approach combined with nonlinear entropy analysis. The study included 20 young adults and 20 older adults. We simultaneously recorded EEG and fNIRS data during four cognitive tasks (auditory attention task, verbal fluency task, upper limb motor task, and recognition memory task). We calculated sample entropy (SampEn) and conditional entropy (CondEn) for five EEG frequency sub-bands (Delta: 1-4 Hz, Theta: 4-8 Hz, Alpha: 8-12 Hz, Beta: 12-30 Hz, Gamma: 30-40 Hz) as well as for fNIRS signals (oxygenated hemoglobin and deoxygenated hemoglobin, HbO and HbR) to quantify neural and hemodynamic complexity of brain activity. Additionally, cross-sample entropy (Cross-SampEn) and cross-conditional entropy (Cross-CondEn) between EEG and fNIRS signals were computed to evaluate NVC function. Group differences were assessed using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), with age group as the fixed factor and sex and years of education as covariates. Older adults showed higher EEG SampEn or CondEn in selected frequency bands during the auditory attention task and the encoding and recognition phases of the recognition memory task. For fNIRS, older adults showed lower HbO SampEn during memory recognition. Cross-modal analysis showed lower beta-HbR Cross-SampEn during the left upper limb motor task and higher theta-HbR Cross-SampEn during memory encoding in older adults. Aging is associated with task-specific alterations in neural complexity, hemodynamic complexity, and the cross-modal temporal relationship between EEG and fNIRS signals. These findings suggest that age-related changes in NVC-related dynamics are better characterized as dynamic reorganization rather than a uniform enhancement or impairment, and support the potential of multimodal entropy analysis for characterizing age-related neurovascular coupling change.

papers.title: Associations between circadian-related behaviors and light exposure and depressive and anxiety symptoms among college students: A cross-sectional study of 10, 630 students from 4 universities.
papers.abstract: Depression and anxiety are highly prevalent among Chinese college students, whose circadian systems face chronotype-schedule mismatch, altered light exposure, and pervasive screen use; the joint associations of these factors with symptoms remain unclear. In a cross-sectional survey of 10,630 students from four Chinese universities, chronotype (rMEQ-5), social jetlag, daytime sunlight exposure, nighttime artificial light exposure (ALAN), and pre-sleep phone use were self-reported; depressive and anxiety symptoms were assessed with the PHQ-9 and GAD-7. Analyses comprised school fixed-effects linear regression with multiple imputation (m = 10), restricted cubic splines, latent profile analysis, and isotemporal substitution models. In fully adjusted single-exposure models, evening chronotype (β = 2.06, 95% CI 1.76-2.35), social jetlag (0.30/h), ALAN (0.22/SD), and pre-sleep phone use (0.33/30 min) were associated with higher PHQ-9 scores, and daytime sunlight (-0.11 per h/d) with lower scores (all P < 0.05); GAD-7 associations were directionally consistent at half the magnitude. Chronotype associations were nonlinear and concentrated in the evening range; the daylight association attenuated beyond ≈2.5 h/d. A long pre-sleep phone plus high social jetlag class scored 0.74 and 0.40 points higher than the high-daylight class. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; exposures were self-reported. Evening chronotype, social jetlag, nighttime light exposure, and pre-sleep screen use were associated with higher, and daytime sunlight with lower, symptom scores; the long pre-sleep phone plus high social jetlag class showed the highest scores; swapping 30 min of pre-sleep phone use for sunlight or sleep was associated with lower PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores, warranting prospective confirmation.

papers.title: Role of External Factors in the Severity of Dissociation Experienced by Treatment- Resistant Depression Patients Following Esketamine Administration.
papers.abstract: Esketamine nasal spray is an NMDA receptor antagonist which is FDA approved, in conjunction with an oral antidepressant, for treatment- resistant depression (TRD) in adults. Dissociation is a well-known side effect to treatment and can be measured using the CADSS (Clinician Administered Dissociative States Scale). To date, patient specific factors that may contribute to the severity of dissociation have not been described. This case series describes two patients receiving treatment with 84-mg esketamine nasal spray twice weekly in an outpatient clinic for TRD who experienced an episode of significant dissociation several months into their treatments. History obtained prior to esketamine treatment included an assessment for any recent stressors. CADSS score was assessed posttreatment. Case 1 was a 55-year-old female who had been receiving esketamine for over two months who presented to the clinic complaining of recent sleep-deprivation while caring for her newborn grandchild. Patient experienced extreme dissociation following administration of esketamine, verbalizing that she felt "very big" and began twitching, grimacing, moaning, and repeating nonsensical statements. CADSS score after treatment was 27. Case 2 involves a 59-year-old female with a remote history of sexual trauma who was four months into esketamine treatments when she presented to the clinic feeling sad after listening to another sexual assault victim's testimony on social media prior to treatment. Shortly after receiving esketamine, she began experiencing a flashback to previous trauma and screaming loudly. CADSS score after treatment was 21. Although both patients reported a history of dissociation with esketamine treatments in the past, they both reported that the level of dissociation they experienced during the above sessions was far more severe. Severe episodes of dissociation during treatment with esketamine in patients with TRD may be associated with patient specific factors. Assessing patients for the presence of recent stressors or changes to their routine prior to each treatment session may help healthcare professionals predict the risk of severe dissociation and allow providers to better prepare to support patients during these experiences. papers.title: Multiscale EEG network alterations in adolescents with depressive symptoms: static-dynamic connectivity, topological features, and exploratory scalp-level network hubs.
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a critical period for brain network development and a vulnerable stage for the emergence of depressive symptoms Although altered brain connectivity has been reported in depression, the multiscale organization of resting-state EEG networks in adolescents with depressive symptoms (ADS) remains insufficiently understood. In particular, conventional network analyses are often constrained by fixed thresholding strategies and single-level observations, which may obscure scale-specific and topology-related abnormalities. Eyes-closed resting-state EEG data were collected from 96 adolescents with depressive symptoms and 154 healthy controls. A data-driven adaptive thresholding strategy was used to construct subject-specific brain functional networks. Static functional connectivity, dynamic functional connectivity, and higher-order topological features were analyzed across macro-, meso-, and micro-scale levels. A multidimensional abnormality convergence matrix was further constructed to explore the spatial correspondence between network abnormalities and exploratory scalp-level neuromodulation hubs. ADS showed scale-dependent abnormalities in brain network organization. At the macro- and meso-scale levels, abnormalities were mainly characterized by theta-band static hyperconnectivity, particularly involving central-region networks, together with reduced dynamic transition flexibility involving prefrontal systems. Micro-scale analysis further localized these alterations to specific connections and nodes. Static connectivity abnormalities were mainly observed along the midline prefrontal-central axis, including Fp1/Fz-FCz connections, whereas dynamic instability was mainly found in right prefrontal-occipital pathways, including Fp2/F4-Oz connections. Higher-order topological analysis indicated vulnerability of right prefrontal nodes, particularly Fp2 and F4. The convergence matrix showed spatial overlap between abnormal network features and the approximate scalp projections of prefrontal neuromodulation sites, while also identifying FCz and Oz as additional nodes that may warrant further investigation. This study provides a multiscale EEG network characterization of adolescents with depressive symptoms. The findings suggest that ADS-related network alterations may involve coexisting compensatory connectivity changes, reduced dynamic flexibility, and focal topological vulnerability. These results may help refine network-level features and provide hypothesis-generating computational references for future studies exploring individualized neuromodulation strategies in adolescents with depressive symptoms.

papers.title: Beyond Exploration: Heightened Recent Reward Reliance and Midfrontal Sensitivity to Outcome Differences in ADHD
papers.abstract: Adaptive decision-making requires balancing the exploitation of known rewards with the exploration of alternative options, yet how attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) shapes this trade-off remains unclear. Using a restless four-armed bandit task and electroencephalography (EEG), we investigated the neural correlates of exploratory decisions and how recent rewards shape choice behavior and feedback processing in 23 adults with self-reported clinical ADHD diagnoses and 27 controls. Across 450 trials with dynamically changing payoffs, choices were classified against the highest last-observed payoff, and behavioral modeling quantified the influence of reward history on subsequent decisions. Contrary to our predictions, exploration rates, task performance, and neural differentiation between exploration and exploitation did not differ significantly between groups. However, adults with ADHD were more likely to repeat an option after high reward feedback and switch after low rewards, driven primarily by the immediately preceding outcome. At neural level, ADHD participants also showed greater midfrontal sensitivity to unsigned changes between consecutive payoffs, expressed in a feedback-evoked response spanning 280 to 568 ms and carried by slow activity below 2 Hz. Together, these findings dissociate the raw frequency of exploration from the dynamic weighting of recent outcomes in ADHD. Rather than reflecting an indiscriminate drive for novelty, behavior was characterized by heightened recent reward reliance paired with amplified slow-wave midfrontal sensitivity to outcome shifts. Crucially, this profile emerged without compromising overall performance, suggesting that, in this volatile environment, ADHD was associated with an increased weighting of recent outcomes rather than with a performance deficit.

papers.title: Oral breathing and its dental and cognitive implications: a structured narrative review with a pediatric focus.
papers.abstract: Oral breathing is a common condition, particularly in pediatric populations, that has been independently associated with dental abnormalities and cognitive dysfunction. However, these outcomes are often studied separately, limiting a comprehensive understanding of their potential interconnection. This structured narrative review synthesizes current literature to examine both the dental and cognitive consequences of habitual oral breathing and to highlight their possible shared physiological mechanisms, including a hypothesized role of disrupted nasal nitric oxide signaling. A structured PubMed search was conducted in October 2024 using two targeted strategies: one focused on dentofacial health outcomes and another on neurological and cognitive effects. Twenty-three primary studies were included in the evidence synthesis (fourteen dental and nine cognitive), and five reviews and editorials were consulted as contextual background. Across multiple studies, oral breathing is associated with malocclusion, differences in craniofacial morphology, and increased risk of oral disease. Concurrently, research suggests associations with reduced working memory, attention difficulties, altered brain oxygenation patterns, sleep-disordered breathing, and decreased academic performance. By setting these findings side by side, this review proposes a hypothesis-generating framework in which oral breathing is considered a possible marker of broad developmental and physiological risk; no included study examined dental and cognitive outcomes in the same participants. These findings emphasize the importance of early interdisciplinary identification and intervention, particularly within pediatric dental care, and highlight the need for future research exploring causal pathways between respiratory patterns, oral health, and cognitive development. Findings should be interpreted in light of the review's limitations, including reliance on a single database for the primary searches, heterogeneity in the diagnostic criteria for oral breathing, the predominance of observational designs, the absence of a formal risk-of-bias assessment, and reliance on adult experimental studies for several cognitive findings.

papers.title: Perioperative esketamine and postoperative sleep quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials.
papers.abstract: Postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) is common among surgical patients and adversely affects recovery. The benefits of perioperative esketamine on sleep remain incompletely defined. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing ketamine or esketamine with saline or other drugs for postoperative sleep quality were identified through a systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library until 6 September 2025. The primary outcome was postoperative sleep quality scores, and effect sizes were calculated using the ratio of means (ROM). Secondary outcomes included incidence of PSD, postoperative pain and depression scores, and adverse events. Twenty-three trials including 2868 participants met inclusion criteria. Esketamine improved sleep quality on postoperative day (POD) 1 (ROM, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.80 to 0.90; P < 0.001; I2 = 84%; 21 studies), POD 2 (ROM, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.57 to 0.93; P = 0.01; I2 = 92%; 8 studies), POD 3 (ROM, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.90 to 0.99; P = 0.02; I2 = 25%; 12 studies), and POD 7 (ROM, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.82 to 0.95; P = 0.001; I2 = 36%; 8 studies); no benefit was observed at 1 month. The incidence of PSD was reduced on PODs 1 through 3 (RRs, 0.71, 0.70, and 0.61, respectively; all P ≤ 0.01), with no effect on POD 7. Esketamine also lowered postoperative pain and depression scores. However, it increased drowsiness (RR, 12.64; 95% CI, 6.04 to 26.46; P < 0.001; I2 = 21%). Perioperative esketamine is associated with short-term improvements in postoperative sleep quality and a lower incidence of PSD, alongside reductions in pain and depressive symptoms. However, these benefits are accompanied by an increased risk of drowsiness, and the current evidence does not yet support routine clinical use. Larger multinational trials are warranted.

papers.title: Symptom-Level Comorbidity Patterns Between Depression and Internet Gaming Disorder Among Adolescents: Evidence from Longitudinal Network Analysis with Gender Considerations.
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a period with an increased risk for the co-occurrence of depression and Internet gaming disorder (IGD), yet we still know little about how specific symptoms of these two conditions influence each other over time. In this study, we applied cross-lagged panel network analysis to two-wave data from a community sample of 538 adolescents (Mean age = 12.51 years; 53.7 percent female). Potential gender differences in the network structure were examined. In the overall sample and in both gender groups, depressive symptoms consistently predicted later gaming-related problems, whereas no reverse cross-disorder pathways were retained. In particular, suicidal ideation and psychomotor symptoms emerged as bridge symptoms linking depression and IGD, while sleep problems showed moderate outgoing expected influence in the overall symptom network. While boys and girls showed broadly similar patterns, some differences emerged in how specific symptoms were connected and which symptoms were most influential. These findings clarify the longitudinal symptom-level associations between depression and IGD in adolescents, suggesting that addressing key depressive symptoms may help reduce the risk of later IGD.

papers.title: How does circadian preference relate to post-traumatic stress and depressive symptoms in adolescents? A moderating role of gender.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to examine the associations between multidimensional circadian preference indicators and their profiles with PTSS and depressive symptoms, and investigate whether gender moderates these relationships. A cross-sectional school-based survey was conducted among 9305 adolescents from all 22 secondary schools in a county in northern China. Circadian preference were assessed using the Morningness-Eveningness-Stability-Scale improved (MESSi), comprising morning affect, eveningness, and distinctness. Depressive symptoms and PTSS were measured using the CES-D-10 and PCL-5, respectively. Latent profile analysis (LPA)was performed to identify circadian subtypes. Multivariable logistic regression and moderation analyses were conducted, adjusting for sociodemographic, health-related, and behavioral covariates. The prevalence of comorbid PTSS and depressive symptoms was 11.6%. LPA indentified three circadian profiles: Morning-Coordinated (4.37%), Intermediate-Stable (80.65%), and Evening-Fluctuating (14.98%). Compared with the Morning-Coordinated group, the Evening-Fluctuating group exhibited markedly elevated odds of comorbidity, isolated depression, and isolated PTSS. Higher morning affect was protective, whereas eveningness and distinctness were risk factors for all symptom outcomes. Gender significantly moderated these associations: the protective effect of morning affect and the adverse effects of eveningness and distinctness were consistently stronger among female adolescents. Circadian preference disruption, particularly the co-occurrence of evening preference and high diurnal fluctuation, is robustly associated with increased risks of PTSS and depressive symptoms in Chinese adolescents. Girls appear to be more vulnerable to the mental health consequences of circadian dysregulation. These findings highlight the importance of stabilizing daily routines and incorporating circadian health into school-based, gender-sensitive mental health interventions.

papers.title: Habitual sleep duration and spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage: a prospective UK Biobank cohort study with supporting hospital-based neurosurgical data.
papers.abstract: Abnormal sleep duration has been associated with stroke, but evidence specific to spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (sICH) remains limited. We conducted a two-part observational study. The prospective UK Biobank analysis included 314,236 participants free of sICH at baseline, among whom 1,387 developed incident sICH. The supporting cross-sectional hospital analysis included 312 patients with imaging-confirmed sICH and 515 non-ICH neurosurgical controls from Jinjiang Municipal Hospital. Habitual sleep duration was categorized as short (<7 h/day), normal (7-9 h/day), or long (>9 h/day). Cox proportional hazards models [hazard ratios (HRs)] and logistic regression [odds ratios (ORs)] were used, together with restricted cubic splines, additional adjustment for medications, blood pressure, and indicators of prevalent ill health, and multiple imputation of missing data. A systemic inflammatory marker score and interaction analyses with false-discovery-rate correction were examined as secondary, exploratory analyses. Compared with normal sleep, short and long sleep were associated with higher incident sICH risk in the UK Biobank [adjusted HRs 1.14 (95% CI 1.03-1.26) and 1.55 (1.15-2.09)]; the short-sleep association was modest and less robust in sensitivity analyses. Corresponding cross-sectional ORs in the hospital dataset were 1.49 (1.04-2.13) and 2.05 (1.17-3.59), respectively. Restricted cubic splines suggested U-shaped associations in both datasets, with the lowest estimated hazard or odds at approximately 7-8 h/day. Estimates were similar after additional confounder adjustment (HRs 1.10 and 1.43 for short and long sleep, respectively) and multiple imputation (HRs 1.13 and 1.50, respectively). No interaction, including with inflammatory marker burden, remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction, and adjustment for the marker score changed the estimates only modestly. Both short and long sleep duration were associated with higher incident sICH risk in the UK Biobank and higher odds of sICH in the hospital dataset, with stronger and more consistent associations observed for long sleep. Systemic inflammatory markers neither explained nor reliably modified these associations, and because long sleep may partly reflect prevalent ill health, the long-sleep association warrants cautious interpretation. Sleep duration may be a useful marker of sICH susceptibility.

papers.title: Exploring Data Augmentation for Stroke Severity Prediction: How Generative AI Enhances EEG Signal Classification
papers.abstract: In clinical datasets, data augmentation is often avoided because it can remove important unusual values, known as outliers, which are important for understanding diseases accurately. However, clinical EEG datasets often suffer from two key limitations: small sample sizes and class imbalance, which significantly reduce classification performance. To overcome these challenges, this study applies generative AI-based data augmentation techniques with a carefully designed hybrid pipeline that effectively enhances performance even on limited EEG data. Using EEG signals from 50 brain stroke patients, we investigate both traditional oversampling methods (SMOTE and ADASYN) and advanced generative models, including WGAN and WGAN-GP. Our proposed pipeline involves preprocessing EEG recordings, extracting comprehensive statistical and frequency-domain features, applying feature reduction, and evaluating multiple machine learning classifiers. Experimental results show that the combination of SelectKBest feature selection, SVM classifier, and WGAN-GP augmentation achieves the highest classification accuracy of 72%, outperforming other methods. This work introduces a novel hybrid approach for EEG-based stroke severity classification, demonstrating that generative augmentation, when integrated properly, can significantly improve performance on small clinical datasets. To the best of our knowledge, this combination of techniques has not been explored before on any dataset, providing a solid foundation for future research in automated EEG-based stroke diagnosis.

papers.title: Side-to-side and other complex head movements as ictal signs in epilepsy: A video-EEG case series and review of literature.
papers.abstract: Side-to-side head shaking is often considered a distinctive clinical sign that differentiates functional seizures from epileptic seizures; however, it may also occur as an ictal phenomenon in focal epilepsy. We retrospectively reviewed all video-telemetry reports of patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy undergoing presurgical evaluation between 2015 and 2025. All reports were electronically screened for mentioning side-to-side or other complex head movements and the video-EEG of these patients was reviewed and included if associated with ictal EEG changes. Seventeen patients were identified who experienced 631 seizures in total, 201 of which included such movements (median: 2 per patient, range: 1-160). One patient (No. 5) accounted for 79% of these events and represented an outlier. Head movements were predominantly horizontal (93.5%), followed by mixed (5%) and rotatory (1.5%). While small-amplitude movements predominated overall, larger amplitudes were more frequent after excluding the outlier case. In six patients, head movements were the initial observed feature of seizure semiology and typically represented a brief component of the seizure, although prolonged in the outlier case. Interrater agreement ranged from fair to good across semiological variables. Presumed epileptogenic zones were heterogenous, including frontal, temporal, anterior quadrant, and hemispheric regions. Ictal side-to-side and other complex head movements can occur in focal epilepsies but lack localizing or lateralizing value. They likely reflect seizure propagation and involvement of broader neuronal circuits. Further studies are needed to clarify their mechanisms and clinical significance.

papers.title: Optimizing aprocitentan dosing in elderly Chinese patients with resistant hypertension: a PBPK/PD-circadian rhythm modeling study.
papers.abstract: Aprocitentan is a dual endothelin receptor antagonist for resistant hypertension (RH), but its optimal use in elderly Chinese patients remains unclear. This study aimed to develop an integrated physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK)/pharmacodynamic (PD)-circadian rhythm model to suggest precision dosing and administration-time optimization in this special population. A PBPK model was developed using published clinical pharmacokinetic data and linked to a direct-effect sigmoid maximal effect model. Circadian blood pressure (BP) variation was described by a triple-harmonic cosine function. After validation against independent pharmacokinetic (PK) and PD datasets, the model was extrapolated to elderly Chinese patients by incorporating age-related physiology, uridine 5'-diphospho-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 activity variability, and mild hepatic impairment. Sensitivity analyses and simulations were performed to evaluate exposure, BP response, and dosing time. The model showed acceptable predictive performance. Sensitivity analyses indicated that aprocitentan exposure was mainly influenced by ionization-, binding-, and distribution-related parameters. Plasma unbound fraction and liver volume were the major determinants of cumulative and steady-state area under the curve (AUC), while lipophilicity predominantly affected early exposure, mean residence time, and terminal half-life. Compared with healthy elderly Caucasian subjects, simulated steady-state AUC increased by 20.6% in elderly Chinese patients and by 52.5% in those with mild hepatic impairment. Among the simulated regimens, 6.25 mg once daily provided the most balanced exposure profile and maintained AUC and maximum plasma concentration within the prespecified reference range in both populations. The model identified 12:00-13:00 as an alternative administration window associated with a favorable simulated 24-hour BP profile. Under the model-predicted regimen, simulated reductions in systolic BP/diastolic BP were 13.04/8.97 mmHg in elderly Chinese RH patients and 13.63/9.37 mmHg in those with mild hepatic impairment, with 24-hour BP remaining mainly within the Grade 1 hypertension range. This study established an integrated PBPK/PD-circadian rhythm model for aprocitentan in elderly Chinese patients with RH. The simulations identified 6.25 mg once daily and midday administration as candidate strategies for further clinical evaluation. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective PK/PD, ambulatory BP, safety, adherence, and clinical validation before implementation in clinical practice.

papers.title: Restorative free time and psychological distress among employed family caregivers of individuals with cognitive impairment: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Employed family caregivers of individuals with cognitive impairment often need to balance work responsibilities, caregiving tasks, and their own daily lives. Although caregiving burden is commonly discussed in terms of time spent caregiving, less attention has been paid to whether caregivers have enough time to recover from these demands. This study examined the associations of daily time-use factors, including restorative free time, sleep duration, working hours, and caregiving duration, with psychological distress among employed family caregivers of individuals with cognitive impairment. A cross-sectional study was conducted as part of the Sustaining for Aging Dementia Relatives Support and Employment project in Japan. Questionnaires were distributed to family caregivers, and data from 210 employed caregivers were analyzed. Psychological distress was assessed using the Kessler 6 scale. Modified Poisson regression with robust variance estimation was used to estimate prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the associations between daily time use and psychological distress. In supplementary analyses, logistic regression was used to explore factors associated with severely limited restorative free time (<1 h/day), including care recipient characteristics such as functional status and long-term care certification. Caregivers with less than 1 h of restorative free time per day had a significantly higher prevalence of psychological distress than those with 3 h or more. Short sleep duration (<6 h/day) was also associated with a higher prevalence of psychological distress, whereas working hours and caregiving duration were not significantly associated with psychological distress after multivariable adjustment. Severely limited restorative free time and short sleep duration were associated with a higher prevalence of psychological distress among employed family caregivers. Limited restorative free time may therefore serve as a potential marker of psychological distress in this population. However, the cross-sectional design does not establish the temporal or causal direction of these associations.

papers.title: Ethical Risks and Governance of Consumer Electroencephalography-Based Neurotechnology: Qualitative Interview Study With Expert Stakeholders
papers.abstract: Background Consumer electroencephalography (EEG)-based neurotechnologies are rapidly expanding across commercial digital health delivery networks and wellness markets. Positioned at the intersection of non-medical self-monitoring and clinical applications, these consumer devices introduce complex challenges for device governance and digital bioethics regarding product claims, data privacy, evidential substantiation, and user protection. Objective This qualitative study examined expert stakeholder perspectives on the ethical, regulatory, and data governance challenges of consumer EEG neurotechnology, focusing on the allocation of responsibility across product lifecycles. Methods We conducted semi-structured interviews with 19 expert stakeholders spanning research, clinical practice, engineering, industry, ethics, law, and regulatory policy across North America, Europe, and Latin America. Interview data were systematically analysed using reflexive thematic analysis to examine how governance challenges, evidence burdens, and responsibilities are conceptualized across the neurotechnology ecosystem. Results Five interrelated themes emerged: (1) Regulatory Category Boundaries and Oversight; (2) Evidential Credibility and Claims-Related Harm; (3) Neurodata Privacy, Security, and Inference; (4) Layered Governance and Explicit Accountability; and (5) Participation, Global Equity, and Contextual Responsiveness. Participants identified major friction in applying traditional medical oversight to nonmedical digital health uses, linked unverified claims to user vulnerability, and expressed concern over downstream neurodata processing. A connecting synthesis demonstrates that oversight responsibilities span multiple actors and development stages rather than resting on a single regulatory mechanism. Conclusions Effective governance of consumer EEG digital health devices requires explicit allocation of duties for claims substantiation, data practices, and user safety, backed by inclusive stakeholder participation and contextual responsiveness.

papers.title: Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome in an elderly female: A video-based case report and literature review.
papers.abstract: Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome (OMAS) is rare in adults. Here, we report a rare case of OMAS in an elderly patient, accompanied by video documentation and a comprehensive literature review, which may offer valuable insights into the clinical features, diagnosis, and management of this condition. An 81-year-old female was admitted with limb tremors lasting for 1 day. During the hospitalization, she developed opsoclonus, myoclonus, ataxia, behavioral changes, and sleep disturbances. Laboratory and imaging findings were unremarkable, with no tumor detected during follow-up, supporting a diagnosis of idiopathic OMAS. Immunotherapy consisted of steroids, while symptomatic treatment included clonazepam and gabapentin. The patient showed marked symptomatic improvement after immunotherapy. At two-year follow-up, there was no evidence of recurrence or malignancy. In elderly patients, OMAS is extremely rare and often diagnosed and treated late. Comprehensive screening for malignancies and infectious triggers is critical. Early recognition and prompt immunotherapy improve outcomes.

papers.title: Association between an improved positioning management strategy and non-incisional low back pain and sleep quality in patients undergoing modified radical mastectomy for breast cancer: a retrospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Non-incisional low back pain, particularly low back pain, and sleep disturbance are common yet underrecognized problems during early recovery after breast cancer surgery. This study evaluated whether an improved positioning management strategy was associated with reduced non-incisional low back pain and improved postoperative sleep quality. This single-center retrospective cohort study included adult women who underwent modified radical mastectomy or simple mastectomy for breast cancer between January 2024 and December 2025. Patients were grouped according to whether an improved positioning management strategy was implemented during the perioperative period (intervention vs. control). Non-incisional low back pain was assessed using the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS, 0-10), and sleep quality was assessed using the Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire (RCSQ: 0-100) at 24, 48, and 72 h postoperatively. Safety outcomes included total drainage volume during the first 3 postoperative days, subcutaneous seroma, and skin-flap ischemia or necrosis. Linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts were used for repeated measures, adjusting for age, body mass index (BMI), analgesic regimen, and postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), with Holm correction for multiple comparisons. Gamma regression and Firth-penalized logistic regression were applied for safety outcomes. Baseline characteristics were generally comparable between groups, although BMI was slightly higher in the intervention group (P = .04) and was adjusted for in multivariable analyses. Improved positioning management was associated with significantly lower non-incisional low back pain (β = -0.711, P < .001). Pain increased over time in the control group, whereas significant group-by-time interactions indicated greater pain reduction in the intervention group at 48 h (β = -0.358, P = .002) and 72 h (β = -0.737, P < .001). Between-group differences in pain at all time points remained significant after Holm correction. The association remained significant after additional adjustment for incisional pain. Improved positioning management was also associated with higher postoperative sleep quality, with significant group and group-by-time effects at 24-72 h. No significant between-group differences were observed in drainage volume, seroma, or flap ischemia/necrosis. An improved positioning management strategy was associated with reduced early postoperative non-incisional low back pain and better sleep quality after breast cancer surgery, without evidence of increased drainage- or flap-related complications. These findings should be interpreted as observational associations and warrant confirmation in prospective studies.

papers.title: Quantifying Academic Risk Factors for Student Depression Using WHO Frameworks: Odds Ratios, SHAP Explainability, and Tipping Point Analysis
papers.abstract: Depression has become a serious concern for students worldwide. Aligned with the WHO Helping Adolescents Thrive (HAT) Guidelines and the Social Determinants of Health (SDoH) model, this study isolates five academically relevant factors- academic pressure, work/study hours, study satisfaction, sleep duration, and financial stress- from a dataset of 27,880 university students in India and quantifies their associations with depression. Unlike prior work that maximises classification accuracy, this study prioritises interpretability: logistic regression provides odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals, Random Forest (RF) and XGBoost rank predictors by feature importance, and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values extend the analysis to individual-level risk explanation. Sleep Duration is encoded as an ordinal integer (0-3) preserving its natural order, and Spearman correlations are computed on the original 27,880-row dataset prior to any resampling. SMOTE oversampling was applied exclusively to the training set, and performance was evaluated on the original imbalanced test set (n = 5,576). Both ensemble models achieve approximately 77-78% accuracy and an AUC of 0.845, confirmed by 5-fold pipeline cross-validation (CV AUC [~] 0.843). Academic pressure is the dominant risk factor (OR = 2.271; RF importance = 0.481; mean |SHAP| = 0.174), while study satisfaction (OR = 0.796) and sleep duration (OR = 0.835) are protective. Interaction analysis reveals how depression risk is amplified by low sleep, high financial stress, and extended study hours: under average conditions, the 50% risk threshold is crossed at Academic Pressure {approx} 3.04, and under compounded adverse conditions, this tipping point shifts to even lower pressure values. These findings provide data-driven thresholds aligned with WHO-endorsed modifiable determinants to support early detection and institutional counselling.

papers.title: Effect of neurofeedback-assisted mindfulness training on migraine severity, associated disability, sleep quality, and emotional distress: protocol for a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Migraine is a highly prevalent neurological disorder and a leading cause of worldwide disability, exerting significant clinical, social, and economic burdens. While pharmacological options exist, their efficacy is often limited by tolerability issues and risk of medication-overuse headache. Neurofeedback (NF) combined with mindfulness training has emerged as a promising non-pharmacological neuromodulation technique. However, clinical evidence in migraine management remains limited by methodological heterogeneity and small sample sizes. This study protocol aims to evaluate the efficacy of a Neurofeedback-Assisted Mindfulness Training Program (NAMTP) in adults with medium-to-high-frequency episodic migraine. This is a randomized, parallel-group, controlled clinical trial protocol. Sixty-six (N = 66) adults diagnosed with medium-to-high-frequency episodic migraine (5-14 monthly migraine days) will be recruited and randomized (1:1 ratio) into either the Intervention Group (IG: standard care plus NAMTP) or the Control Group (CG: standard routine care alone). The IG will undergo a 12-week home-based program consisting of 60 sessions (15-20 min each, 5 times per week) of mindfulness training assisted by the Muse® electroencephalography (EEG) headband. Assessments will be conducted at baseline, 12 weeks (post-intervention), and 24 weeks post-randomization. The powered primary outcome is the change in Monthly Migraine Days (MMDs). Secondary outcomes include migraine-associated disability (MIDAS), headache impact (HIT-6), sleep parameters (actigraphy and PSQI), quality of life (MSQ v.2), and mood symptoms (BDI-II and STAI-Y). This protocol addresses the urgent need for scalable, non-pharmacological therapies in migraine management. By combining objective neurophysiological monitoring with behavioral training within a rigorous randomized controlled framework, this trial will clarify whether NAMTP can reduce headache burden, optimize sleep patterns, and diminish affective distress. The findings are expected to provide standardized, actionable evidence regarding the integration of digital neurofeedback tools into routine clinical care for episodic migraine.Clinical Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07661888.

papers.title: Prevalence of Overweight and Obesity and Their Associations With Screen Time and Other Behavioral Factors Among Adolescents in the United Arab Emirates.
papers.abstract: Background Overweight and obesity among adolescents are major public health concerns. Sociodemographic, familial, dietary, and lifestyle factors, including screen time and physical activity, may be associated with excess body weight. In the United Arab Emirates (UAE), limited evidence has examined recreational screen time alongside these factors in the same adolescent population. Objective This study aimed to determine the prevalence of overweight and obesity among adolescents aged 14-18 years in the UAE and examine whether greater recreational screen time was associated with higher odds of overweight/obesity. Secondary analyses assessed associations of sociodemographic, familial, dietary, physical activity, and sleep factors with overweight/obesity. Methodology A cross-sectional study included 688 adolescents aged 14-18 years recruited from participating high schools and a university teaching hospital in the UAE between December 2023 and April 2024. Height and weight were measured by the investigators, and BMI was classified using sex- and age-specific WHO 2007 growth reference cutoffs. Participants completed a structured questionnaire assessing sociodemographic characteristics, family history, dietary habits, physical activity, screen time, and sleep. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson chi-square tests, and binary logistic regression. Results The prevalence of combined overweight/obesity was 39.8% (95% CI: 36.2-43.5%); 27.3% (95% CI: 24.0-30.7%) were overweight, and 12.5% (95% CI: 10.0-15.0%) were obese. Although weekend non-academic screen time was associated with overweight/obesity in the chi-square analysis (p = 0.017), no screen-time category was significant in bivariable logistic regression. In multivariable analysis, overweight/obesity was associated with male sex (AOR = 1.636, 95% CI: 1.155-2.318; p = 0.006), family history of obesity (AOR = 2.014, 95% CI: 1.197-3.389; p = 0.008), frequent eating when not hungry or bored (AOR = 1.884, 95% CI: 1.012-3.509; p = 0.046), and no participation in ≥60 minutes/day of out-of-school moderate-to-vigorous physical activity on any day of the week (AOR = 1.896, 95% CI: 1.285-2.799; p = 0.001). Conclusions Overweight and obesity were common among adolescents in this study. Recreational screen time was not associated with overweight/obesity in the regression analysis. Male gender, family history of obesity, frequent eating when not hungry or bored, and no participation in ≥60 minutes/day of out-of-school moderate-to-vigorous physical activity were associated with overweight/obesity after adjustment. Given the cross-sectional design and recruitment from participating schools and a university teaching hospital, these findings represent associations rather than causal relationships and are not nationally representative of UAE adolescents.

papers.title: Cogwheel Rigidity in Subacute Combined Degeneration Unresponsive to Vitamin B12 Therapy.
papers.abstract: Parkinsonian symptoms seen with B12 deficiency have been described in five cases where B12 therapy has led to their elimination. Subacute combined degeneration (SCD) presenting with parkinsonian signs of cogwheel rigidity, unresponsive to B12 supplementation, has not heretofore been described. Case Study: This 62-year-old right-handed woman with a past medical history of hypothyroidism presented with complaints of trouble with memory. Cogwheel rigidity and pernicious anemia with low intrinsic factor and B12 levels (165 pg/ml) were found. SCD was diagnosed and treated with monthly B12 injections over the past three years, providing symptomatic relief, yet the cogwheeling persisted. She described never developing trouble with gait, movement disorders, autonomic abnormalities, olfactory dysfunction, disorders of sleep, visual hallucinations, or other parkinsonian symptoms. Abnormalities in Neurologic Examination: Cranial Nerve (CN) Examination: CN I: Alcohol Sniff Test: 9 (hyposmia). CN III, IV, VI: Bilateral ptosis. Motor Examination: 1+ Cogwheel rigidity both upper extremities. Drift Testing: Right pronator drift with left abductor digiti minimi sign. Reflexes: 3+ throughout other than 4+ ankle jerks. Quadriceps femoris bilaterally pendular. Bilateral Hoffman and Babinski reflexes present. B12 Level: 394 pg/ml (normal). While predominantly affecting the posterior columns and the lateral corticospinal tract, the demyelination may further extend into adjacent fibers including the reticulospinal tract and the rubrospinal tract, the tracts which, in Parkinson's Disease, have been cited for their role in maintenance of tone and thus cogwheeling. Additionally, low B12 and elevated homocysteine levels have been noted as potential contributory factors in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's Disease. It is also possible that this is a violation of Occam's razor, that this individual has two separate distinct diseases - the prominent subacute combined degeneration as well as a subclinical parkinsonism which was revealed on neurologic examination. The parkinsonian signs may have been present prior to the B12 deficiency, and if not for the examination findings, could have remained undiscovered for decades. In those that present with Subacute Combined Degeneration, evaluation for parkinsonism is warranted. No Funding.

papers.title: Cardiovascular Health Promotion for US Veterans: Current State, Gaps, and Strategies: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association.
papers.abstract: US veterans represent a large and diverse population with distinctive demographic characteristics, comorbidity profiles, and social determinants of health shaped by military service. These factors contribute to a high burden of cardiovascular risk and low attainment of ideal cardiovascular health. At the same time, the Department of Veterans Affairs, which operates the nation's largest integrated healthcare system, provides a unique infrastructure for delivering population-level cardiovascular disease prevention for veterans. Understanding its successes and ongoing challenges can inform broader strategies across all health systems for promoting health among veterans. This scientific statement applies the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 framework, expanded to include mental health and substance use, to evaluate veteran cardiovascular health. For each domain, we review guideline recommendations, barriers to achieving optimal health, and major Veterans Affairs programs such as Patient Aligned Care Teams, the MOVE! Weight Management Program for Veterans, Whole Health, telehealth-based interventions, and integrated mental health and substance use disorder services. Across domains, veterans receiving Veterans Affairs care often achieve outcomes that are equal to or better than those of their non-Veterans Affairs counterparts, reflecting the strengths of the system in coordinated, team-based care and research-driven implementation. Despite substantial progress, opportunities remain to improve veteran lifestyle behaviors, metabolic health, lipid and blood pressure control, engagement in mental health and substance use care, and detection and management of sleep disorders. Addressing these challenges at the Veterans Affairs will require continuing to expand care access, enhancing digital data integration, tailoring interventions to high-risk subgroups, and strengthening implementation strategies to improve uptake and engagement across Veterans Affairs services.
