papers.title: Aviation Medicine and Cardiovascular Assessment of Aircrew: A European Society of Cardiology-Aligned Review of Integrating International Civil Aviation Organization, European Union Aviation Safety Agency, Federal Aviation Administration, and Turkish Directorate General of Civil Aviation Aeromedical Standards.
papers.abstract: Aeromedical certification is based on a safety-first principle: a pilot or other aircrew member must not have a medical disorder that creates an unacceptable risk of sudden or subtle incapacitation during flight. Cardiovascular disease remains one of the most important determinants of flight fitness, as it may impair consciousness, judgment, rhythm stability, exercise capacity, and hemodynamic reserve. Modern aeromedical decision-making therefore requires the integration of aviation law, operational risk, contemporary cardiology guidelines, advanced imaging, biomarkers, and long-term surveillance. The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Annex 1 provides the global licensing framework; the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) Part-MED, together with its Acceptable Means of Compliance and Guidance Material, defines detailed operational standards in Europe; and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) employs a protocol- and special issuance-based system for many cardiovascular and metabolic disorders. This review summarizes the aeromedical assessment of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic and acute coronary syndromes, heart failure, cardiomy-opathies, arrhythmias and conduction disorders, pacemakers and implantable cardiac devices, valvular heart disease, aortic disease, congenital heart disease, venous throm-boembolism, cardiovascular pharmacotherapy, and major respiratory conditions rel-evant to flight certification. The manuscript is aligned with current European Society of Cardiology cardiovascular guidance and with the operational aeromedical principles applied by ICAO, EASA, FAA, and the Turkish Directorate General of Civil Aviation. In general, preserved ventricular function, absence of significant symptoms, low thrombo-embolic and arrhythmic risk, stable treatment, and adequate exercise capacity support certification or restricted certification. In contrast, uncontrolled hypertension, unstable diabetes, significant residual myocardial ischemia, reduced ejection fraction, malignant ventricular arrhythmias, implantable defibrillator therapy, severe valvular disease, significant aortic pathology, major congenital hemodynamic lesions, or poorly controlled sleep apnea usually preclude certification. Final decisions remain individualized and depend on license class, operational role, treatment burden, surveillance data, and the judgment of the aeromedical authority.

papers.title: Can COVID-19 Cause Acute Psychosis in Pediatric Patients? A Case Report.
papers.abstract: To demonstrate that COVID-19-associated acute psychosis, though rare, can happen in the pediatric patient population. Patients with new-onset psychosis should be tested for COVID-19 infection, and other organic causes of psychosis should also be considered (e.g., delirium, medication-induced psychosis, and catatonia). Patient X, a 14-year-old female with no known past psychiatric history, presented to the local emergency room following odd behavior for 3 days and having tested positive for COVID-19 2 weeks prior. The patient's mother reported odd behaviors, including the patient claiming her fish was calling her name and her name was being repeated on TV. She had been moving slowly with occasional staring. The patient's mother reported episodes in which the patient was repeating phrases over and over and where she would require redirection to a task. When the patient planned to have a bath, her mother noted that she was naked in her room while looking for something and then needed redirection to go take a bath. She did not have any episodes of agitation. A thorough psychiatric evaluation indicated she was experiencing visual hallucinations. Her vitals were within normal ranges, except for a mildly elevated heart rate. The patient was admitted for further testing, assessment, and management. She was started on chlorpromazine 10 mg daily as needed for psychosis. A complete blood count with differential (CBC), complete metabolic panel (CMP), and thyroid function results were all within the normal range. Urine drug screening was negative. EKG, CSF analysis, chest X-ray, and brain MRI showed no significant abnormalities. Mild background slowing was noted on EEG, with no interictal/epileptiform discharges or any delta brushes. Therefore, a tentative diagnosis of COVID-19-associated psychosis was made. Treated with chlorpromazine 10 mg daily, the patient gradually improved with no hallucinations or bizarre behavior. She was discharged after 5 days and was not prescribed any medication at discharge. Nine days after discharge, the patient was seen by a pediatric neurologist. She did not report any hallucinations or delusions, but her mother reported that the patient moved slowly and had difficulty identifying common objects. An autoimmune panel, physical exam, and repeat EEG were all unremarkable. The neurologist concluded that her psychosis was most likely post-viral sequelae. The patient continued to improve and returned to school over the span of 2 months. Acute psychosis after COVID-19 infection is a new and emerging diagnosis with no consensus on management strategies for pediatric or adult patient populations. This case highlights the need for clinicians to be vigilant of subtle, fluid psychotic symptoms, in addition to patients' general mental well-being. We do not have research regarding the long-term consequences of acute psychosis episodes. Further studies are needed to investigate the neuropsychiatric etiology of post-COVID-19 psychosis and the optimum treatment for this group of patients. No Funding.
